item.title: REFLECTION I Seeking refuge in the mask
item.description: This poem was composed from a challenging perspective, as it was written about a friend who shared the trials and tribulations of a sad life journey with me. item.content:encoded:
This poem was composed from a challenging perspective, as it was written about a friend who shared the trials and tribulations of a sad life journey with me. Alas, she resides abroad and I felt that my offer of comfort and compassion towards her situation was subdued in depth due to our distance.

Thus, the inspiration for this poem as an Ode to her true character – her dedication to duty, her resolve to stay through the years rather than walk away and even today, live life with a face of Grace, despite enduring many chapters of conflict.

People seek recourse to a mask for many reasons.

Some attempt to conceal negative energy – a narcissistic personality.

Some seek refuge in a mask as a medium for healing a hurt heart, without attention or detection.

Others may seek recourse to a mask to preserve and protect their positive energy – a face of serene silence in the midst of turbulent tides that wash their way.

The poem sought to assure a long-suffering heart that there are people with eyes that see. There are people with ears that listen. There are people with minds that reflect from observation the reality of a situation.

It is a life of torment for those who live a life confined within a frame and a test for those who walk beside their path in faithful friendship. The conviction of their conditioning – often self-inflicted from doubt and depression – is referred to as ‘Belief Perseverance’ in social psychology and sadly, a perplexing phenomenon which provides an explanation on why some people are protective of their initial beliefs.

They preserve their beliefs even when offered new, truthful and sometimes contradictory avenues and evidence to change the course of their life path. Indeed, it is a challenge to convince them to heal from within of their own accord and in their own time. Nonetheless, an understanding of the belief bias system is an aid to understanding their social sensitivity and delicate decision-making process.

The principal perspectives of belief perseverance focus on two key factors:

1. Cognitive dissonance – people feel distress due to holding two or more opposing beliefs.

2. Confirmation bias – to eliminate feelings of distress, people may neglect new beliefs that are not aligned to their current beliefs. Thus, they dismiss advice and evidence that can restrain and resolve a negative situation.

My friend neither sought professional assistance and intervention or shared her experiences with anyone, until our correspondence matured with time. Her solution was to seek refuge in Nature and continue to be the soldier on duty, as per her belief system from childhood socialisation.

I composed the poem as a personal initiative to instigate healing from within and hopefully, she would realise her worth one day to initiate positive change. Unfortunately, as time passed, I noted that the belief perseverance syndrome was so well imbedded in her personality that it was akin more to an infestation – waves of negative emotions would invade her mind on a regular basis to the extent that she withdrew into episodes of deep depression.

Before I composed the poem, I appended a card to my regular correspondence. It was a plain card with a message I only came to realise later, would create a profound impact. The message read: “You Are Enough.” That was the only sentence on the card. The response to me was: “Thank You.”

I was both surprised and pleased by the response I received because it relayed to me many words unspoken. She likely received that message for the first time in her life and after reflecting on her response, I composed the poem.

Suffice to say, she has chosen the path of self-healing.

item.title: FOCUS I A farewell in song – As Pacific treasures prepare for a new chapter
item.description: Prayer, song and dance echoed through the South Australian Museum’s Pacific Cultures Gallery as Pacific communities gathered not to say goodbye forever, but to honour the beginning of a new journey. The occasion, known as the Melanesian Lullaby, marked an emotional milestone for one of Australia’s most significant collections of Pacific cultural heritage.
item.content:encoded:
Prayer, song and dance echoed through the South Australian Museum’s Pacific Cultures Gallery as Pacific communities gathered not to say goodbye forever, but to honour the beginning of a new journey.

The occasion, known as the Melanesian Lullaby, marked an emotional milestone for one of Australia’s most significant collections of Pacific cultural heritage.

Hosted by the Papua New Guinea Association of South Australia in partnership with the South Australian Museum, the gathering symbolised a gentle farewell as thousands of treasured cultural objects entered a planned period of rest and conservation.

Like the lullaby that inspired the event, the ceremony represented comfort, protection and care, a promise that the stories carried by the objects would continue long after they leave public view.

From Monday, August 3, 2026, the Pacific Cultures Gallery temporarily closed after decades on display, beginning a major conservation and cultural care program that the Museum says will protect the collection for generations to come.

The gallery had remained open until Sunday, August 2, allowing visitors one final opportunity to experience the exhibition before work commenced.

The South Australian Museum houses Australia’s largest collection of Pacific material, with around 3,000 bows, arrows, spears, shields, utensils, ornaments, masks and ritual objects from Papua New Guinea, the Solomon and Santa Cruz Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji and New Zealand.

Rather than marking an end, museum leaders say the closure signals the start of a new chapter.

South Australian Museum director Dr Samantha Hamilton said the decision reflected the Museum’s responsibility to care for objects that hold deep spiritual and cultural significance.

“I’ve had the privilege of being taught by elders and by youths on the importance of cultural materials,” she said.

“My role here at the museum is to bring all cultures together and to create a space where the South Australian community, but also the people of Australia, can share stories, knowledge and respect for each other’s culture.

For Dr Hamilton, the collection represents far more than museum pieces.

“These objects absolutely represent spiritual and cultural values, the power of the people who created them and so it’s our responsibility to now be able to put these objects to rest,” she said.

“They have been on display for decades. The wonderful Centennial Hut has been on display since 1936 and it’s time to be responsible and actually put it to rest so that future generations can also protect, preserve and learn from it.”

The conservation program will be undertaken in partnership with local Pacific communities, ensuring cultural authority, traditional knowledge and ceremonial protocols guide the care and stewardship of ancestral objects.

While the gallery doors have temporarily closed, Dr Hamilton stressed that public access to knowledge will continue through extensive documentation and digital technology.

“We are going to be creating digital records for people, for things that are in storage,” she said.

The Museum plans to create high-resolution 3D digitisations of objects, allowing people to continue engaging with the collection while conservation work progresses.

The reopening, planned for the coming years after the conservation program is completed will feature stronger community voices, broader representation of Pacific cultures and more contemporary storytelling.

For Adelaide resident and community leader of the Fijian Association of South Australia, Luke Qovu Junior, the Museum’s approach recognises what these objects truly represent.

“It is a great initiative by the South Australian Museum to preserve these cultural items for the future,” he said.

“Whilst embarking on this project they have collectively involved Pasifika communities that have strong connections and values to these artefacts, which hold profound cultural and ancestral significance to them, especially us Fijians.”

Mr Qovu said the collection carried meaning that extends far beyond history.

“For many Fijians, these artefacts represent more than history. They connect families to their provinces, villages, mataqali and yavusa. They remind us of the values passed down through generations, respect, service, courage, unity and faith.”

He said each object served as a tangible connection between past and present.

“They are physical reminders of who we are and where we come from. They are living connections to our ancestors.

“They tell the story of our people, our vanua, our customs and traditions, our way of life, our spirituality, our craftsmanship, our chiefs, our provinces, our kingdoms and the many generations that shaped the Fiji we know today.”

He said the Fijian community looked forward to working alongside the museum during the next stage of the project.

Hosted by the Papua New Guinea Association of South Australia in partnership with the South Australian Museum, the gathering symbolised a gentle farewell as thousands of treasured cultural objects entered a planned period of rest and conservation. Picture: SOUTH AUSTRALIAN MUSEUM / SIA DUFF

The conservation program will be undertaken in partnership with local Pacific communities, ensuring cultural authority, traditional knowledge and ceremonial protocols. Picture: SOUTH AUSTRALIAN MUSEUM

item.title: OUR FASCINATING WORLD I Weather and climate measuring
item.description: In the Pacific, rain is never just weather; it is life, sustenance, and sometimes a sudden, overwhelming force. You can smell it on the trade winds long before it arrives—that unmistakable, earthy scent of petrichor rising off the warm soil as heavy cumulonimbus clouds darken the horizon. item.content:encoded:
In the Pacific, rain is never just weather; it is life, sustenance, and sometimes a sudden, overwhelming force. You can smell it on the trade winds long before it arrives—that unmistakable, earthy scent of petrichor rising off the warm soil as heavy cumulonimbus clouds darken the horizon.

Yet, for all its familiar presence, quantifying liquid water from the sky is one of meteorology’s greatest logistical challenges. How do we turn a torrential tropical downpour or a persistent drizzle into exact millimetre records that farmers, hydrologists, and disaster managers can trust?

Following our look at the wind, this second part of our series explores the essential instruments that capture the Earth’s most vital fluid, tracing water from the open clouds down to the rain gauge and into our climate archives.

At its most fundamental level, measuring rain requires a reliable container and a graduated cylinder. Standard rain gauges used across meteorological networks are essentially open-ended cylinders designed with a precise funnel area to catch rainwater while preventing loss from splashing or evaporation.

When a shower passes, the collected water is poured into a narrow measuring tube where even a fraction of a millimetre becomes visibly magnified.

While deceptively simple, these manual gauges have served island communities for generations, providing the crucial baseline data needed to understand local microclimates and seasonal water availability without relying on complex electronics.

To capture rainfall in real time—especially during remote operations or fast-moving storms—meteorologists rely on the ingenious tipping-bucket rain gauge. Inside a cylindrical housing, rainwater funnels down into a tiny, balanced see-saw dual bucket mechanism.

Once exactly 0.2 millimetres (or 0.01 inches) of rain fills the active side, the weight tips the bucket over, dumping the water out the bottom while simultaneously moving the second bucket into place.

Each physical “tip” triggers a tiny magnetic reed switch that sends an electrical pulse to a data logger or telemetry transmitter. This transforms continuous rainfall into an instantaneous stream of digital data, letting forecasters track downpour intensity minute by minute.

In heavy tropical squalls or long-duration monsoonal events, standard tipping buckets can sometimes under-report intense rainfall rates because water splashes out or drains too quickly during extreme peaks. To solve this, high-precision climate stations utiliSe weighing-bucket precipitation gauges.

Instead of counting tips, the entire catchment bucket sits atop a sensitive mechanical scale or load cell. As rain accumulates, the total weight increases continuously, recording every drop regardless of whether it falls as light mist, heavy rain, or even melting hail. This continuous weight curve provides a foolproof historical trace of accumulation over hours and days.

While rainfall is our primary tropical concern, global precipitation encompasses solid forms like snow, sleet, and ice pellets in higher latitudes or high altitudes.

Measuring solid precipitation requires heated gauge attachments that melt frozen water as it falls so it can pass through the standard measuring mechanism.

For climatologists tracking global water cycles, knowing the water equivalent of solid precipitation is just as vital as measuring tropical rain. Unheated gauges left to catch snow would quickly clog and freeze, missing critical accumulation data entirely during cold-weather events.

One of the greatest hidden enemies of accurate rain measurement is the wind. When strong winds blow across an open weather station, they create swirling eddies around the top of a rain gauge, blowing light droplets or fine rain sideways and drastically underestimating the true catch.

To combat this aerodynamic error, professional rain gauges are surrounded by specialized wind shields—such as the Alter shield, featuring a ring of freely swinging metal slats that deflect approaching wind downward and smooth the airflow over the instrument opening. Without these shields, high-wind storms like tropical cyclones would severely compromise rainfall data accuracy.

Ground gauges give us hyper-accurate point measurements, but rain never falls evenly across an entire island or ocean. To see the big picture, meteorologists look to weather radar and environmental satellites.

Ground-based radar sends out pulses of electromagnetic energy that bounce off falling raindrops. By analysing the strength of the returning echo, radar systems create real-time, color-coded maps showing exact rain intensity and storm movement across hundreds of kilometres.

Satellites complement this from above, tracking cloud-top temperatures and moisture bands to estimate precipitation over vast, unpopulated ocean spaces where no ground gauges can ever go.

The millimetre measurements collected by rain gauges directly drive the economic heartbeat of the islands. Farmers rely on antecedent rainfall data to decide when to plant, irrigate, or harvest crops, balancing soil moisture against evaporation rates.

Meanwhile, hydrologists use cumulative precipitation tracking to monitor river catchments and dam storage levels. When a gauge records sudden multi-day precipitation spikes, it triggers vital flood warnings, protecting downstream villages and infrastructure before flash floods sweep through river valleys.

Every isolated millimetre of rain measured in a backyard gauge or automated station feeds directly into the global hydrological cycle equations. Meteorological centers assimilate these numbers to calculate regional water balances—comparing incoming precipitation against runoff and evaporation.

These large-scale insights help scientists understand how atmospheric moisture transport systems, such as the South Pacific Convergence Zone (SPCZ), distribute fresh water across maritime nations, influencing everything from local municipal water security to regional agriculture planning.

Beyond daily forecasts and flood alerts, long-term precipitation records are a cornerstone of climate change science. Decades of consistent rain gauge data allow climatologists to detect shifting wet seasons, prolonged drought cycles, and intensifying rainfall extremes driven by a warming atmosphere.

As global temperatures alter evaporation rates and moisture holding capacity in the clouds, maintaining meticulous, unbroken precipitation archives ensures we can model future water security risks.

Through simple gauges and advanced satellites alike, we track the ancient rhythm of the rain to secure our resilience in a changing world.

Dr Sushil K Sharma BA MA MEng (RMIT) PhD (Melbourne) — World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) Accredited Class 1 Professional Meteorologist. Former British Aerospace, The Royal Saudi Air Force and Bahrain Air Navigation Directorate Aviation Meteorologist. Former Associate Professor of Meteorology, Fiji National University, and Operational Meteorologist and Manager, Climate Research and Services Division, Fiji Meteorological Services. item.title: BACK IN HISTORY I Women learn new skills
item.description: MORE than 40 women from Macuata district gathered at Bulileka Village to learn small-scale business skills by building a kitchen. A report in The Fiji Times on May 16, 1986, said the week-long course taught women how to construct a simple kitchen and furnish it with locally made materials. The project was sponsored by the International Labour Organization, which contributed $400.
item.content:encoded:
MORE than 40 women from Macuata district gathered at Bulileka Village to learn small-scale business skills by building a kitchen.

A report in The Fiji Times on May 16, 1986, said the week-long course taught women how to construct a simple kitchen and furnish it with locally made materials. The project was sponsored by the International Labour Organization, which contributed $400.

The course was conducted by government workers Salanieta Rika and Nacanieli Lutu and participants came from Sasa, Labasa, Dogotuki, Namuka, Nadogo and Udu districts.

Ms Rika said the women adapted the building materials during the course.

“Initially, the women were supposed to use bamboo to build the walls of the kitchen, but since the village had some timber, we decided to use it instead,” she shared.

They were also taught to build their own smokeless stoves and sinks.

She said the kitchen would make daily life easier.

“This project benefit the women because when the menfolk come home late at night after a yaqona session, they do not have to disturb the women to heat the food.”

She said the skills could also support income-earning.

“The women would make things like jam and cakes to sell in a small business operation.”

item.title: TOURISM TALANOA | The reality of building towards 4000 rooms
item.description: Fiji’s tourism industry is in the middle of one of the most ambitious accommodation expansions this country has seen in years – which might be a good problem to have. item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s tourism industry is in the middle of one of the most ambitious accommodation expansions this country has seen in years – which might be a good problem to have. Government has set a target of roughly 4000 additional hotel rooms to support a goal of 1.25 million visitors and four billion dollars in tourism earnings by 2027, with the tourism minister pointing to accommodation capacity as the constraint that must grow to support rising demand.

Ambition of that kind should be welcomed, and I say that as someone who represents an industry that has spent years arguing that Fiji’s growth potential exceeds its current bed stock. But ambition on its own does not build a hotel or fill it with skilled staff and visitors hungry for local experiences. It is important, therefore, to discuss just how we’re actually tracking against that target, and on the one issue that continues to determine whether these numbers translate into rooms on the ground rather than plans, or half-finished construction sites, sitting idle for months and sometimes years.

Delivered supply between 2025 – 2027 will amount to 1800 rooms in total – from eight rooms in the North to the eventual opening of The Westin’s 246 rooms and 27 suites along with the Vatu Talei (127 rooms and 48 suites) in Denarau, The Sebel Nukuloa’s 76 rooms in Wailoaloa (slated to open this year), and the Radisson Mirage in Naisoso – all reflecting real confidence from operators and developers willing to commit capital to this market. Once construction is confirmed for at least another five small to medium resorts in 2027, we can expect a steady, but realistic increase in room inventory by 2030 of approximately 500 a year. If we’re lucky, that might translate to around 3300 rooms. By 2030.

That’s our honest, but basic math calculations, because we believe our infrastructure and supply networks deserve straight numbers rather than a rounded-up sense of progress. Governments’ own recently announced tourism construction progress figures, which should be the cleanest yardstick available, showed sixteen projects under construction as of June 2025, expected to deliver just over 2200 additional rooms against that stated need of around 4000 by 2027. That means, on Government’s own accounting, roughly 2200 of the 4000 rooms needed were in construction as of the middle of last year, leaving a gap of about 1800 rooms still to be committed and built. While that is a meaningful contribution to the 2200 under construction, it is nowhere near the full 4000 required, and the Westin situation is a live reminder that even projects already counted in that 2200 figure are not guaranteed to land on schedule.

The remainder is presumably spread across the balance of what Government has described as a fifty-three-project pipeline worth around three billion dollars, most of which have not had individual room counts confirmed in public reporting. And we have not seen a published running tracker of rooms delivered against rooms needed, so any percentage figure attached to this progress is our own calculation from the numbers available, not an official statistic, and should be read with that caveat in mind.

None of this is a criticism of the ambition itself. It is simply a reminder that the gap between a stated target and delivered rooms is still wide, and that the projects in between a groundbreaking ceremony and an opening night are where the real story of this expansion actually sits.

Investment Fiji’s own account of the investment climate supports what our members tell us constantly. Fiji has shifted its investment policy toward a more facilitative approach, with a new facilitation committee and digital tools aimed at improving transparency and reducing bureaucracy, and Investment Fiji reports it managed 522 projects worth $F8.7 billion over the past three years.

Of the 212 investment projects currently active, valued at approximately $6.2b, only six are under construction, while 73 sit in pre-development and 53 remain in the planning phase. That is a genuinely strong pipeline of stated interest. It is also a pipeline where the overwhelming majority of projects have not yet moved past planning into anything resembling a foundation being poured.

Government’s own investment climate reporting has for years acknowledged this same pattern, describing general difficulty establishing businesses and implementing large investments as a considerable risk to growth, alongside a welcoming policy environment that nonetheless leaves investors facing lengthy and costly bureaucratic delays before anything gets built.

Such tension requires Government’s frank recognition and a commitment to address it openly. Investment Fiji can say correctly that interest in Fiji as a tourism investment destination is strong. The Ministry of Tourism can say correctly that 4000 rooms are needed and that incentives and infrastructure upgrades are being put in place to attract that capital.

Both of those things can be true, and both are being said with good intention. But an investor does not experience Government as a single, coordinated voice. They experience it as a series of separate desks, each operating under its own timeline, its own interpretation of the rules, and often with limited visibility and even less care into what the desk next door is doing. One ministry can be actively courting an investor with talk of streamlined approvals and a facilitative new posture, while a completely separate arm of the civil service sits on that same investor’s paperwork for months, working through a process that has not caught up with the message being sold at the front door.

It is the exact experience FHTA hears about repeatedly, from operators who have expressed genuine interest in opening a hotel or extending an existing one and have found themselves stuck navigating exactly this kind of internal disconnect.

This is why Ease of Doing Business remains one of the things we consistently fight hardest for, and what that actually means is not asking for shortcuts or for paperwork to disappear (this happens without our input). Proper documentation should still be filled out and filed correctly, and due diligence should still be done properly.

What we are asking for is that it should not sit on someone’s desk for months gathering dust while an investor waits, follows up, waits again, and eventually loses interest in Fiji altogether and takes their capital somewhere with a faster answer. We say smoother deliberately, not easier. Those are two different things that Government understands the difference between too, even if the machinery does not always reflect it yet.

So here is where we eventually land. I am genuinely optimistic about what this room expansion could mean for Fiji’s tourism sector, and the openings already delivered over the past three years prove this is not just talk.

But optimism has to be matched with internal coordination that investors can actually feel, not just hear about in a conference address, and with honest reporting when projects hit real difficulty along the way.

If Government’s target of 4000 rooms is going to translate into 4000 rooms rather than a headline figure that quietly slips past 2027, the right hand and the left hand of the civil service need to know what each other is doing and be held accountable.

An investor’s file needs to move through that system with the same energy that goes into announcing the target in the first place. That is not too much to ask of a country that already knows, better than most in this region, exactly how much tourism is worth to it.

n FANTASHA LOCKINGTON is the CEO of the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association. The views expressed are not necessarily those of The Fiji Times. To share a comment or thoughts on the article, please send an email to info@fhta.com.fj

item.title: BACKTRACKS I Keeping traditions alive
item.description: LAST week we looked at the revival of the traditional yaqona (kava) chant known as Cila na Siga Va Vula Lima by villagers of Navakuru in Labasa, led by the Tui Labasa, Ratu Jone Qomate. One of the most powerful messages of the ceremony came from those who represented its future.
item.content:encoded:
LAST week we looked at the revival of the traditional yaqona (kava) chant known as Cila na Siga Va Vula Lima by villagers of Navakuru in Labasa, led by the Tui Labasa, Ratu Jone Qomate.

One of the most powerful messages of the ceremony came from those who represented its future.

Four young members of the chiefly family participated in the revival. They were Ratu Jone’s son, Ratu Sakiusa, together with Ratu Roqica Qomate and his brothers, Ratu Joji and Ratu Kelepi.

Their involvement demonstrated that cultural preservation is not solely the responsibility of elders. It is a responsibility that must be shared by every generation.

“Their participation symbolised the passing of our traditions from one generation to the next,” Ratu Jone said. “Seeing young members of the chiefly family embrace their cultural responsibilities gave everyone hope that these customs will continue to live on.”

Across Fiji, many communities continue to grapple with the challenge of preserving traditional knowledge in a rapidly changing world. Modern technology, migration and changing lifestyles have made it increasingly difficult for younger generations to learn traditional ceremonies, accompanying chants and associated protocols. Many customs that were once common are now practised only occasionally while some have already disappeared.

For traditional leaders such as Ratu Jone, this makes cultural preservation more important than ever.

“As a traditional chief of the vanua of Labasa, I believe it is my personal duty and responsibility to ensure that our customs, traditions and protocols continue to be upheld,” he emphasised.

“These traditions are an important part of our identity and should never be allowed to disappear. They connect us to our ancestors and teach our young people the importance of respecting their culture.”

Culture, he believes, is not something that belongs only in museums or history books. It must remain a living part of everyday community life. That means songs and chants must continue to be sung. Ceremonies must continue to be performed. Traditional knowledge must continue to be taught.

The revival of Cila na Siga Va Vula Lima is therefore about much more than preserving a chant. It is about strengthening identity. It reminds people of where they come from and reinforces the values that have united the vanua o Labasa for generations.

Every performance carries stories of ancestors who built the foundations of today’s communities. Every verse reflects respect, humility and unity. Every ceremony strengthens the bond between people and their vanua.

Ratu Jone hopes the revival will inspire other villages to revisit their own traditional practices. Many communities possess songs, chants and ceremonial customs that have not been performed for years. Some survive only in the memories of the elderly. He believes those traditions deserve renewed attention before they disappear completely.

“I hope this revival inspires other villages within the vanua of Labasa to preserve and practise their own traditional chants and ceremonies,” he added.

“Our culture is one of our greatest treasures, and it is our collective responsibility to protect it.”

He said teaching these traditions to children today would ensure they continued long into the future. The revival also highlighted the important role elders play in protecting indigenous knowledge.

Without their dedication, the chant may have vanished completely. Instead, they quietly carried its lyrics through the years until the next generation is ready to receive them.

Their commitment reflects a broader truth about culture. Traditions survive because people choose to preserve them. They require patience, teaching and participation. They also require opportunities for younger people to experience them firsthand rather than simply read about them.

Watching the young stand proudly alongside their elders during the ceremony offered reassurance that the future of the tradition remains strong. It is a reminder that culture flourishes when knowledge is shared, responsibilities are embraced and young people are given the chance to lead.

For Ratu Jone, preserving cultural practices is about honouring those who came before while preparing those who will follow.

“By teaching these traditions to our children today, we ensure they will remain alive for many generations to come,” he said. “Reviving our cultural practices strengthens the identity of our people and reminds us of where we come from. It encourages young people to take pride in their heritage and appreciate the wisdom handed down by their elders. Cultural traditions also foster unity within the vanua by bringing families and communities together through shared customs and ceremonies.

“If we fail to preserve these practices, future generations may lose an important part of their history and identity. By keeping our traditions alive today, we honour the sacrifices of our ancestors while ensuring that the unique customs of the vanua o Labasa continue to flourish for generations to come.”

As the final notes of the yaqona chant echoed through the gathering, it was clear that the revival represented far more than the return of a forgotten tradition. For the vanua of Labasa, Cila na Siga Va Vula Lima had reclaimed its rightful place in one of the most important cultural ceremonies of the vanua.

Its revival showed the determination of a chief to preserve their heritage and the willingness of a new generation to embrace the customs entrusted to them. It was a reminder that culture is kept alive not only through memories, but through practice, participation and the passing of knowledge from one generation to the next. As long as these traditions continue to be taught and honoured, the spirit of the vanua of Labasa will endure, carrying its history, identity and values into the future.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY I Fete for a queen
item.description: Ba celebrated the success of its first major community carnival in 1996, raising more than $60,000 for community projects and crowning a new carnival queen as the sugar town looked to reinvent itself beyond its traditional reliance on the sugar industry. According to The Fiji Times of September 18, 1996, 21-year-old DAV College teacher Christabel Taylor, of Ba Riverside, was crowned Ba Carnival Qu
item.content:encoded:
Ba celebrated the success of its first major community carnival in 1996, raising more than $60,000 for community projects and crowning a new carnival queen as the sugar town looked to reinvent itself beyond its traditional reliance on the sugar industry.

According to The Fiji Times of September 18, 1996, 21-year-old DAV College teacher Christabel Taylor, of Ba Riverside, was crowned Ba Carnival Queen after impressing judges and the community throughout the festival.

Sponsored by the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), Ms Taylor also claimed the Miss Charity title after raising $18,000. FSC also won the award for the best float during the carnival’s final-day parade.

Reflecting on her victory, Ms Taylor said the support she received from the people of Ba had exceeded her expectations.

“I am a newcomer to the town but the response from the people was marvellous. I have a lot of new friends now and the people just accepted me as one of them. This was very important to me.”

She said her mother would accompany her on her prize trip during the Christmas holidays.

Ms Taylor also encouraged more young women to take part in community carnivals.

“People should not enter with the wrong attitude. Sometimes people criticise you behind your back. But they don’t appreciate what you do for them,” she said.

“They come out expecting to be treated as a queen. You should look forward at enlarging your mind.”

Formerly known as the Bougainvillea Carnival, the festival attracted seven contestants competing for the crown.

Ba mayor Pradeep Chand described the event as a success, despite falling short of its $100,000 fundraising target.

item.title: Top Executive Conference 2026 | Platform for leaders
item.description: The Fiji Commerce & Employers Federation (FCEF) is excited to bring you the Top Executive Conference (TOPEX) 2026 – Fiji’s premier business event – from November 19–21 at the Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa, Denarau. Now in its 12th year, TOPEX continues to provide a national business platform where those who lead, influence, invest, regulate and build businesses come together to listen, share and contr
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Commerce & Employers Federation (FCEF) is excited to bring you the Top Executive Conference (TOPEX) 2026 – Fiji’s premier business event – from November 19–21 at the Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa, Denarau.

Now in its 12th year, TOPEX continues to provide a national business platform where those who lead, influence, invest, regulate and build businesses come together to listen, share and contribute to the conversations shaping Fiji’s economic direction.

Reflecting on the role TOPEX has come to play, FCEF vice president and TOPEX committee chair Rowena Taito said: “TOPEX has become a cornerstone event for Fiji’s business community, recognised for bringing the right people into the room.”

“It provides a platform for business leaders of all sizes, investors, policymakers, decision-makers, development partners and industry voices to discuss the issues that matter to enterprise and contribute to conversations about Fiji’s economic future.”

Fiji continues to see potential across tourism, trade, investment, infrastructure, technology, green growth, MSME development, regional partnerships and new areas of enterprise.

However, these opportunities do not automatically become growth.

They require confidence, coordination, practical policy settings and a private sector that is ready to lead.

This is where TOPEX continues to play an important role.

The conference provides a space for honest, practical and constructive conversations — centred on the issues that sit close to every business owner’s reality – bottlenecks, policy, regulations, operating costs, investment opportunities, productivity, market access, partnerships and networks.

Some of the most valuable insights often come not only from formal presentations, but from the experiences shared by other business owners who face similar pressures, testing new ideas, entering new markets, managing teams, navigating regulation and finding ways to grow.

For large businesses, TOPEX offers the opportunity to understand emerging trends and connect with the wider private sector ecosystem.

For MSMEs and growing enterprises, it provides access to the thinking, networks and experiences of more established businesses.

For all delegates, it creates space to step back from day-to-day operations and think more strategically about the future.

Building on last year’s format, TOPEX 2026 will feature relevant, engaging and forward-looking conversations grounded in the interests and experiences of Fiji’s business community.

The team are carefully curating a programme that brings together business leaders, policymakers, technical experts and experienced practitioners who can share practical insights, introduce fresh perspectives and contribute meaningfully to the discussion.

As businesses respond to changing workforce needs, new technologies, emerging markets, regulatory developments and climate considerations, it is important to create opportunities to exchange experiences and consider what these changes could mean for enterprise.

The program is still taking shape and will be shared once it has been finalised.

Visit our website fcef.com.fj to get the latest.

TOPEX 2026 will once again be held at the Sofitel Fiji Resort & Spa, Denarau, from November 19 to 21, 2026.

This year, participant numbers have been limited to maintain the quality of engagement and the overall conference experience. Businesses and organisations interested in attending are strongly encouraged to register early.

Registrations for TOPEX 2026 are now open.
